title: b, d, f, k, l, m, n, p, t, v, z sound much as in English
body: These letters are close to English when they are pronounced. d, t, n and l are made with the tongue against the upper teeth, and l is always the clear “l” of “leaf”, even at the end of a word (il, ville). m and n are only plain consonants before a vowel; otherwise they make the vowel nasal.

title: French words have no strong stress
body: English hammers one syllable in each word; French gives every syllable about the same weight and length. Do not weaken unstressed vowels: say each one clearly, and do not stress the first syllable of words like hôtel or animal.

title: p, t and k sounds have no puff of air
body: English p, t and k at the start of a word come with a small puff of air (hold a hand in front of your mouth and say “pat”). French p, t and the “k” sound have none, so to English ears they can sound close to b, d and g.

title: Final consonants are usually silent
body: Most consonants at the end of a word are not pronounced: the t of petit, the s of vous, the d of grand, the x of deux. The common exceptions are c, r, f and l: remember them as “CaReFuL”. A few short words like bus, sud and ouest also keep their last sound.

title: r is made at the back of the throat
body: French r is made with the back of the tongue near the soft palate, a soft rasp like a gentle gargle, close to the “ch” of Scottish “loch” but voiced. It is never the English r and never rolled with the tongue tip. Say it in every position: pour, merci, très.

title: a is “ah”
body: a sounds like a short “a” in “father”, or a little brighter, between “cat” and “father”. It never becomes the weak “uh” of English “about”. Before n or m that is not followed by a vowel, it turns nasal (see an, en).

title: Final e and -es are silent
body: An e at the end of a word longer than one syllable is not said, and neither is -es: elle sounds like “el”, une like “ewn”. Its job is to make the consonant before it heard: petit ends in “ee”, but petite ends in a clear “t”.

title: Lengthen the last syllable of each phrase
body: The only stress in French falls on the last pronounced syllable of a word group: it is a little longer, not louder. In je voudrais un café, only “-FAY” stands out. A silent final e does not count as a syllable.

title: i, î and y are “ee”
body: i, î and y are the “ee” of “see”, but short and tense, never the “i” of “sit”. y on its own, as in il y a, is also “ee”.

title: an, am, en, em are a nasal “ahn”
body: When n or m is not followed by a vowel, the vowel before it is said through the nose and the n or m itself is not pronounced. an, am, en and em all sound like “ah” through the nose, close to “on” in British “long” without the “ng”.

title: ss and s elsewhere are a hissing “s”
body: ss is always “s” as in “see”, and so is s at the start of a word or next to a consonant: aussi, le sac, reste. In est (is) the s is silent.

title: Before a vowel or a double n or m, the vowel is not nasal
body: If n or m is followed by a vowel or doubled, the vowel stays plain and the n or m is pronounced: un (nasal) but une “ewn”, bon but bonne “bon”, an but année “ah-NAY”. A few words starting with emm- or enn- stay nasal: emmener, ennuyer.

title: é sounds like “ay” in “say”
body: é is a clear, tight “ay” with no glide at the end, as if you stopped “say” before the “ee”. It is always pronounced, even at the end of a word: parlé and parle sound different.

title: e before two consonants or a final c, f, l, t is “eh”
body: An e followed by a double consonant, two different consonants, x, or a pronounced final consonant is the “e” of “bed”: elle, merci, reste, avec. Before n or m with no vowel after it, e turns nasal instead (see an, en).

title: je, le, de, que: the e is a short “uh”
body: In the little one-syllable words je, me, te, se, le, ce, de, ne and que, the e is a short “uh” said with rounded lips. Before a vowel these words lose their e and join the next word (j’ai, l’eau).

title: o is “oh”, or the “o” of “lot” before a sounded consonant
body: At the end of a word or before a silent consonant, o is a pure, closed “oh” with no “w” glide: le vélo, le mot. Before a pronounced consonant it is more open, like the “o” in British “lot”: la porte, l’homme.

title: u is “ee” said with rounded lips
body: French u has no English equivalent: say “ee”, keep the tongue there, and round your lips as for “oo”. Do not turn it into “oo”: tu (you) and tout (all), dessus and dessous are different words. The respellings write it “ew”.

title: c, r, f and l at the end are usually pronounced
body: Remember “CaReFuL”: these four letters are usually said at the end of a word, unlike the others. The big exception is -er, which is silent in verbs and most other words (see that rule). A few words drop the c, like blanc and tabac, and the l of gentil and outil is silent.

title: c before a, o, u or a consonant is “k”
body: Elsewhere c is the “k” of “cat”: le café, comme, la classe. In second the c is said like “g”: “suh-GOHN”.

title: ai and ei sound like “e” in “bed”
body: ai, aî and ei are one sound, the “eh” of “bed”: mais is “meh”, la neige is “lah NEZH”. At the end of a verb, -ai is closer to “ay”: j’ai is “zhay”. Before l or ll, as in travail and soleil, see the “y” rule.

title: Double consonants are said as one
body: Unlike Italian, French doubled letters are not held longer: elle is “el”, la pomme “lah POM”, attendre “ah-TAHN-druh”. Doubling often just shows that the vowel before it is not nasal (bonne) or that s stays “s” (poisson).

title: A final consonant links to a vowel in the next word
body: A pronounced final consonant, or one before a silent e, slides into the next word if it starts with a vowel, as if the two were one word (enchaînement): il est is “ee-LEH”, elle a “eh-LAH”, avec elle “ah-veh-KEL”.

title: ou sounds like “oo” in “food”
body: ou, où and oû are the “oo” of “food”, short and with rounded lips. Keep it apart from u: vous (you) is “voo”, but vu (seen) has the French u.

title: on and om are a nasal “ohn”
body: on and om, with no vowel after them, are a rounded “oh” said through the nose, without a real n. Keep the lips round. The odd one out is monsieur, said “muh-SYUH”.

title: e between single consonants is a weak “uh”, often dropped
body: An e followed by one consonant and a vowel is a short “uh” as in “about”, with rounded lips. In everyday speech it is often left out when only one consonant comes before it: samedi is “sahm-DEE”, maintenant “mant-NAHN”.

title: An apostrophe joins two words into one
body: Before a vowel or mute h, short words like le, la, je, de, ne, que and si drop their vowel and attach to the next word: l’eau is “loh”, j’ai “zhay”, qu’il “keel”, s’il “seel”. Say them as a single word.

title: i before a vowel glides into “y”
body: An i before another vowel becomes a quick “y” sound in the same syllable: bien is “byan”, le pied is “luh PYAY”. A y at the start of a word before a vowel does the same: les yeux.

title: -ais, -ait, -aient all sound like “eh”
body: These verb endings (je parlais, il parlait, ils parlaient) all sound the same, “eh”: the s, t and -ent are silent. Only the subject tells you who is meant.

title: qu sounds like “k”
body: qu is a plain “k”, with no “w”: qui is “kee”, quatre “KAH-truh”. The u is silent.

title: les, des, mes, ces end in “ay”
body: In the short words les, des, mes, tes, ses and ces, -es is said “ay” (many speakers say “eh”): les is “lay”, des is “day”. The s is silent unless a vowel follows (see liaison).

title: est sounds like “eh”, et like “ay”
body: est (is) is just “eh”: the s and t are silent. et (and) is “ay”, and its t is never linked to the next word. c’est is “seh”.

title: c before e, i or y sounds like “s”
body: Before e, i or y, c is the “s” of “see”: merci, la cerise. Before a, o, u or a consonant it is a hard “k”.

title: in, ain, ein, im and ien are a nasal “an”
body: in, im, ain, aim, ein and yn sound like the “a” of “bank” said through the nose, with no real n: le vin is “luh VAN”. After i, y or é, en has this sound too: bien is “byan”, européen “uh-roh-pay-AN”.

title: au, eau and ô sound like “oh”
body: au, eau and ô are all a pure, closed “oh”, with no glide at the end: beau is “boh”, aussi is “oh-SEE”. Do not say the e of eau.

title: à, â, î, û and ù: the accent hardly changes the sound
body: These accents mostly tell words apart in writing: à (to) and a (has), où (where) and ou (or). â can sound a little deeper, like “ah” in “father”; î and û sound just like i and u.

title: è and ê sound like “e” in “bed”
body: è and ê are the open “eh” of “bed”, a little longer in ê. They are always pronounced: très is “treh”, la fête is “lah FET”.

title: j sounds like “s” in “measure”
body: j is always the soft “zh” of “measure”, never the “j” of “jam”: je is “zhuh”, le jour “luh ZHOOR”.

title: -er and -ez at the end sound like “ay”
body: The verb endings -er and -ez, and most other words ending in -er, end in “ay” with the r or z silent: parler, vous parlez, premier. A few short words keep the r and say “ehr”: mer, cher, hier, hiver, fier.

title: oi sounds like “wah”
body: oi and oî are “wah”, as in “wasp”: moi is “mwah”, trois is “trwah”. The one common exception is oignon, said “oh-NYOHN”.

title: A single s between vowels sounds like “z”
body: One s between two vowels buzzes like the “z” in “zoo”: la maison is “lah meh-ZOHN”. Write ss to keep the hissing “s”: le poisson (fish) but le poison (poison).

title: un and um are a nasal “uhn”
body: un and um, with no vowel after them, are traditionally a nasal “uh”. Most people in France now say them like in, a nasal “an”, so both are fine.

title: ch sounds like “sh”
body: ch is the “sh” of “ship”, never the “ch” of “church”: chez is “shay”, le chat “luh SHAH”. In a few Greek words it is “k”: l’orchestre, la psychologue, technique.

title: eu and œu before a sounded consonant are an open “uh”
body: Before a pronounced consonant, eu, œu and œ are more open, like the “u” in “fur” said without any r and with rounded lips: l’heure, la sœur, jeune.

title: g before a, o, u or a consonant is a hard “g”
body: Elsewhere g is the “g” of “go”: le gâteau, la gare, grand. At the end of a word after n it is usually silent (long, le sang), and so is the g of vingt and le doigt.

title: g before e, i or y sounds like “s” in “measure”
body: Before e, i or y, g is the soft “zh” of “measure” or “beige”, never the “j” of “jam”: rouge, la page, le gîte.

title: eu at the end of a syllable is a closed “uh”
body: At the end of a word, before a “z” sound or before one consonant and a vowel, eu and œu are said like “ay” with tightly rounded lips: deux, peu, heureuse. Say “ay”, then push your lips forward into a small circle. The past participle eu (had) is said like the French u instead.

title: ui sounds like a quick “wee”
body: In ui, the French u glides quickly into “ee” in one syllable, close to “wee” but with the lips rounded and pushed forward: huit is “weet”, la nuit is “lah NWEE”.

title: Liaison after les, des, un, mon and other words before a noun
body: A normally silent final consonant is said when the next word starts with a vowel or mute h, and it moves to that word. After articles, mon, ton, son, numbers and adjectives such as petit or grand, liaison is obligatory: les amis “lay-zah-MEE”. s and x sound “z”, d sounds “t”, n is a plain “n”.

title: h is silent
body: h is never pronounced in French: l’hôtel is “loh-TEL”, l’homme “LOM”. Most words starting with h behave as if they started with a vowel, so the article drops its vowel and words link to them.

title: -ent at the end of a verb is silent
body: The verb ending -ent (ils parlent, elles aiment) is not pronounced at all: ils parlent sounds exactly like il parle. In other words -ent is a nasal “ahn”: souvent, le moment, l’argent.

title: Never link after et
body: The t of et (and) is never pronounced, even before a vowel: toi et elle is “twah ay EL”, with a small break and no “t”.

title: Liaison after nous, vous, ils, elles, on and en
body: Subject pronouns link to a verb starting with a vowel: nous avons is “noo-zah-VOHN”, ils ont “eel-ZOHN”, on a “oh-NAH”. Compare ils sont (“eel SOHN”, they are) with ils ont (“eel ZOHN”, they have): the liaison is the only difference.

title: tion sounds like “syohn”
body: In -tion the t sounds like “s”: la station is “lah stah-SYOHN”. After s or x it stays “t”: la question is “lah kes-TYOHN”.

title: plus and tous: s sometimes said
body: plus is “plew” when it means “no more” (je n’ai plus) and often “plews” when it means “more” or “plus”. tous is “too” before a noun (tous les jours) and “toos” when it stands alone (ils sont tous là).

title: ail, eil, euil, ouil sound like a vowel plus “y”
body: After a vowel, il at the end of a word and ill inside it are a “y” glide: travail is “trah-VAHY”, le soleil “luh soh-LEHY”, la feuille “lah FUHY”. The l is silent.

title: six, dix, huit, cinq, sept and neuf say their last consonant
body: On their own, these numbers keep their final sound: six “sees”, dix “dees”, huit “weet”, cinq “sank”, sept “set” (the p is silent), neuf “nuhf”. Before a consonant six, dix and huit often drop it (six jours “see ZHOOR”), and before a vowel they link (dix ans “dee-ZAHN”, neuf ans “nuh-VAHN”).

title: Liaison after dans, chez, très, sans, quand and tout
body: Short words such as dans, chez, sans, très, plus, tout and quand usually link too: dans un an is “dahn-zuh-NAHN”, quand il pleut “kahn-teel PLUH”, tout à coup “too-tah-KOO”.

title: th sounds like “t”, ph like “f”
body: th is a plain “t”, never the English “th”: le thé is “luh TAY”. ph is “f”: la photo is “lah foh-TOH”.

title: k and w appear in borrowed words
body: k and w are found in foreign words and names. k is “k”. w is “w” in English words (le week-end) and “v” in some German ones (le wagon).

title: x inside a word is “ks” or “gz”
body: x is usually “ks” as in “taxi”, and “gz” in ex- before a vowel: exemple is “eg-ZAHMPL”. In deuxième and sixième it is “z”, and in soixante “s”. At the end of a word it is silent.

title: y between vowels works like a double i
body: Between two vowels, y works like “i + i”: the first changes the vowel before it and the second is a “y” glide. payer is “peh-YAY”, voyage “vwah-YAZH”, moyen “mwah-YAN”. Note le pays, “luh pay-EE”.

title: ç is always “s”
body: The little hook under ç turns the c into an “s” before a, o or u: ça is “sah”, le garçon “luh gar-SOHN”.

title: gn sounds like “ny” in “canyon”
body: gn is one sound, like the “ny” in “canyon”: la montagne is “lah mohn-TAHNY”, gagner is “gah-NYAY”. Never say a separate “g”.

title: A few common words break the rules
body: Learn these by heart: monsieur is “muh-SYUH”, femme is “fahm”, second is “suh-GOHN”, the ai of faisons and faisais is “uh”, le pays is “luh pay-EE”, and eu (had) is just the French u.

title: ill after a consonant sounds like “ee-y”
body: After a consonant, ill is usually “ee” followed by a “y” glide, and the l is not heard at all: la fille is “lah FEEY”. A few words keep a real “l”: ville, village, mille, million, tranquille and the city Lille.

title: gu before e or i is a hard “g”; the u is silent
body: The u in gue and gui only keeps the g hard: la guitare is “lah gee-TAHR”, la langue “lah LAHNG”. It is not a “w” sound.

title: Questions often rise at the end
body: A question without a question word is often just a statement with the voice rising on the last syllable: tu viens ? is “tew VYAN?” with a rise. Questions with a question word can fall at the end, as in English.

title: oin sounds like a nasal “wan”
body: oin is “w” followed by the nasal “an” of vin: loin is “lwan”, moins is “mwan”. The n is not pronounced.

title: Some words start with an h that blocks linking
body: A few words start with an “aspirated” h. It is still silent, but it acts like a consonant: no l’, no liaison, no linking. Say le haut, les héros (“lay ay-ROH”), le huit. Learn them as you meet them.

title: ou before a vowel glides into “w”
body: Before another vowel, ou usually becomes a quick “w” in the same syllable: oui is “wee”, jouer is “zhway”, l’ouest is “lwest”.

title: sc before e or i is a plain “s”
body: In sc before e, i or y, the c adds nothing: the pair is one “s” sound. la piscine is “lah pee-SEEN”.

title: cc before e or i sounds like “ks”
body: In cc before e or i, the first c is “k” and the second “s”: accepter is “ahk-sep-TAY”, l’accident “lahk-see-DAHN”.

title: ge before a or o: soft g, silent e
body: To keep g soft before a, o or u, French adds an e that is not pronounced: nous mangeons is “noo mahn-ZHOHN”, il mangeait “eel mahn-ZHEH”.

title: est-ce que sounds like “ess-kuh”
body: The question starter est-ce que is said “ess-kuh”, two quick syllables: est-ce que tu viens ? is “ess-kuh tew VYAN”. qu’est-ce que is “kess-kuh”.

title: ë and ï: say the vowel on its own
body: The two dots on ë or ï mean the vowel is said separately from the one before it: Noël is “noh-EL”, naïf “nah-EEF”, le maïs “luh mah-EES”.

title: -emment and -amment sound like “ah-MAHN”
body: Adverbs ending in -emment and -amment both end in “ah-MAHN”, with a plain “ah”, not a nasal: récemment is “ray-sah-MAHN”.
